Chapter 8: Cultivating Abundance and Overcoming Scarcity Thinking
Have you ever caught yourself thinking there just isn’t enough—whether it’s time, talent, money, or opportunity—to really go after your dreams?
That’s scarcity thinking in action. It’s sneaky, and it can leave you feeling stuck, envious, and even a little hopeless. But here’s the truth: creativity isn’t a zero-sum game. There’s plenty of room for your voice, and for everyone else’s too.
So, what’s the antidote? It all starts with abundance thinking—shifting your focus from what’s missing, to what’s already here and what’s possible. The first step is gratitude. When you start noticing the small joys, the resources you already have, and those sparks of inspiration, your world opens up. Suddenly, taking creative risks feels less scary, and a lot more exciting.
Let’s talk about a few simple ways to bring more abundance into your creative life:
First, try keeping a gratitude list. Every day, jot down three things you’re grateful for—especially the little things that fuel your creativity. Maybe it’s a friend who cheers you on, a new idea that pops up, or just a peaceful moment to work.
Next, practice celebrating others. When someone you know has a creative win, celebrate them—genuinely! Instead of comparing, let their success remind you there’s more than enough to go around.
Another great tool is resource mapping. Make a list of all the things and people that support your creative work—your time, your skills, your materials, and your community. You’ll probably realize you have more support than you thought.
And finally, lean into generosity. Share your encouragement, your feedback, or even your time with others on a creative path. When you give freely, you help build an atmosphere of abundance—and you’ll find it often comes back to you.
Overcoming scarcity thinking isn’t a one-and-done deal. It’s something you practice, especially since we live in a world that loves to push competition and “not enough.” But when you come back to gratitude and generosity, you teach your creative self to trust that there is enough.
And you’ll discover, maybe for the first time, that what you have to offer is not just valuable—it’s needed.
